narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 54.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were your performance in the third year of law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year performance. Your third-year grades were actually the strongest positive influence on the prediction, gently pulling the outcome toward passing. However, this helpful effect was outweighed by two clear drags toward failure: your LSAT score and your first-year grades.

Your LSAT of 32.5 sits noticeably below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, and this gap pushed the model strongly toward expecting you to struggle with the bar. Similarly, finishing in the fourth decile after your first year (compared with an average of sixth decile for accepted students) also pulled the prediction toward failure. Even though your family income, gender, race, planned full-time status, and later improvement in the third year were taken into account, they could not overcome the combined downward pressure from the LSAT and early academic performance.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation and consider strengthening any additional academic credentials before reapplying. These steps would directly address the two features that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
